questions.question_text: A board member objects that a Level 3 adaptive textbook will be costly because "every student's request has to go to a large language model." How does the chapter's design loop answer this objection?

options.A: It agrees, and recommends limiting adaptive textbooks to small pilot classes only
options.B: At use time, adaptation is a lookup using the record, a rule, and the graph
options.C: It shows that the LMS performs the adaptation, so no extra system is needed
options.D: It shows that the MicroSims send each answer to an AI model running in the browser

questions.explanation: The chapter's loop uses a static site, browser-run MicroSims, xAPI statements, a record store, a mastery rule, and a learning graph. No step requires a live large language model. AI may have helped write the content once, but when a student uses the textbook the work is lookups, rules, and a record. That keeps the Level 3 cost per student modest and limits the privacy risk to one bounded record store. The LMS does not perform adaptation in this design.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: What is a foundational concept in a learning graph?

options.A: A concept with no prerequisites, where learning can begin
options.B: A concept that nothing else depends on, which ends a chain
options.C: The concept with the most dependencies pointing to it
options.D: The first concept taught in the first chapter of a course

questions.explanation: A foundational concept has no prerequisites in the graph; it is a root from which everything else grows. This book's graph has 14, including Education, Student, Learning, and Artificial Intelligence. A concept that nothing else depends on is a terminal concept, the opposite. Being first in a course outline or having many dependents does not by itself make a concept foundational.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: Why must a learning graph be a directed acyclic graph?

options.A: Because only acyclic graphs can be drawn in a browser-based viewer
options.B: Because standards bodies require all educational data to use this format
options.C: Because a cycle would make every concept in it a foundational concept
options.D: Because if A required B and B required A, no student could learn either

questions.explanation: A cycle means each concept would have to be learned before the other, which is impossible. Checking for cycles is one of the first quality tests, and this book's graph passes it. The DAG property also guarantees the concepts can always be put in an order where each comes after its prerequisites, which is the basis of a learning path. Concepts in a cycle would all have prerequisites, so none would be foundational.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: Which organization's learning standards include xAPI and Learning Object Metadata?

options.A: The IMS Global Learning Consortium, now 1EdTech
options.B: The Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
options.C: The Society for Learning Analytics Research
options.D: The U.S. Department of Education's What Works Clearinghouse

questions.explanation: The IEEE's Learning Technology Standards Committee maintains learning technology standards, including xAPI (now an IEEE standard, originating with the Advanced Distributed Learning initiative) and Learning Object Metadata, which describes a resource's title, subject, level, and rights. IMS Global, renamed 1EdTech in 2022, produces LTI, OneRoster, QTI, Common Cartridge, and Caliper Analytics. Caliper serves a similar purpose to xAPI, which makes the first option tempting.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: At a rural elementary school, students need a separate login for each of four learning tools, and the free textbook cannot be opened from the district LMS. Which standard addresses both problems?

options.A: OneRoster
options.B: QTI
options.C: LTI
options.D: Caliper Analytics

questions.explanation: Learning Tools Interoperability (LTI) lets an outside tool plug into a learning management system with single sign-on and the ability to return grades, so the tools and the textbook open from inside the LMS with one login. OneRoster exchanges rosters and grades with the student information system, which solves re-typing class lists, not logins. QTI moves quiz questions between systems, and Caliper reports learning events for analytics.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: A district can produce an interactive textbook once for \$30,000, or pay about \$6 per student per year for live AI generation of each student's lessons. Above roughly how many students does generate-once become cheaper for a single year?

options.A: About 5,000 students
options.B: About 500 students
options.C: About 50,000 students
options.D: About 180,000 students

questions.explanation: The two costs are equal when \$30,000 equals \$6 times the number of students, which is 5,000. Above that, the fixed cost of generate-once spreads across more students while live generation keeps growing with every student. The chapter's own example crosses at about 3,100 students and notes that generate-once content can also serve students for several years, while live generation can personalize far more than a fixed book.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: According to the chapter, how does a textbook's level affect whether it works without an internet connection?

options.A: Every level works offline once the student has logged in at least once
options.B: Only Levels 4 and 5 work offline, since the AI model is stored on the device
options.C: Levels 1 and 2 work offline, Level 3 can buffer, and Levels 4 and 5 need a connection
options.D: No level works offline, since all digital textbooks are served from a remote host

questions.explanation: A static website is ordinary files, so it can be saved to a laptop or USB drive or cached by the browser. Levels 1 and 2 therefore work offline, Level 3 can buffer its records and send them later, and live AI chat at Levels 4 and 5 needs a connection to a remote model. The chapter concludes that the choice of level is a connectivity decision. The second option reverses the relationship.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: A school shares a 2 megabit-per-second connection. Twenty students open a 2-megabyte lesson page at the same moment. About how long will it take for all of them to load it?

options.A: About 20 seconds
options.B: About 1 second
options.C: About 8 seconds
options.D: About 160 seconds

questions.explanation: Two megabits per second is 2 / 8 = 0.25 megabytes per second. Twenty students times 2 MB is 40 MB, and 40 / 0.25 = 160 seconds, close to three minutes. Eight seconds is the time for one student alone. Twenty seconds forgets to convert bits to bytes. The chapter shows that a page cached on the school network the night before loads in under a second, so the design, not just the connection, decides the experience.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: Which feature does the chapter identify as a mark of a well-designed student progress dashboard?

options.A: A ranking that shows each student's place in the class
options.B: A next step the student can take, shown alongside their own progress
options.C: A complete list of every click the student made that week
options.D: A points total that rewards students for time spent on screen

questions.explanation: A well-designed dashboard shows a student their own progress, not their place in a ranking, and always shows a next step. Maya's example lists what she has mastered, what is ready next, and a note from her teacher, with no comparison to classmates, no points, and no grade. The chapter warns that rankings can discourage students who are behind and that a long list of clicks drowns the reader in noise.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: A district is choosing between two designs for a remote school with old laptops and a slow shared connection: a live AI chat tutor, or a static textbook with browser-based simulations cached on the school network. Which analysis fits the chapter?

options.A: The chat tutor fits better, since text messages use less bandwidth than any web page
options.B: Both designs perform about the same, since each needs the same connection speed
options.C: The static textbook fails, since browser-based simulations require a fast server
options.D: The static textbook fits: it runs locally and offline, while chat needs a live link

questions.explanation: Static pages and browser-based simulations run on the student's own device with no server doing the computation, can be cached locally, and keep working when the network is down. Live AI chat cannot work offline and needs a network round-trip for each exchange. The chapter warns that testing only on the best connection can widen the equity gap. Browser-based simulations need a capable enough device, not a fast server, so the third option reverses how they work.

questions.chapter: Learning Graphs, Interoperability Standards, and Access at Scale
questions.question_text: A vendor says its product "integrates with everything" through custom integrations but supports none of LTI, OneRoster, or xAPI. What does the chapter suggest the district should conclude?

options.A: The product is a lock-in risk; the district should require standards when it buys
options.B: Custom integrations are better than standards, because they are built for each district
options.C: The district should build its own integration, since standards rarely work in practice
options.D: The product is fine as long as the vendor offers a lower price than competitors do

questions.explanation: Interoperability standards prevent lock-in, lower cost because a tool built once works in every compliant system, and let small open projects take part. The chapter advises asking for standards by name and warns that "custom integrations" usually means extra cost and lock-in. The district does not need to build integrations itself; it needs to require the standards when it buys. A low price does not remove the risk of data trapped in proprietary formats.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: What does COPPA require, and what does the FTC allow schools to do under it?

options.A: It protects education records in federally funded schools, and lets schools share them with any vendor
options.B: It protects EU residents' data, and lets schools process it with no lawful basis
options.C: It protects children under 13 online, and lets schools consent for parents for educational use only
options.D: It protects students over 13 online, and lets schools consent for parents for any purpose

questions.explanation: COPPA requires operators of services directed at children under 13, or that know they collect data from them, to give notice and get verifiable parental consent. The FTC allows schools to consent on behalf of parents for educational uses only, so a school that signs a vendor's terms takes on responsibility for what the vendor does. Commercial uses such as advertising need parental consent a school cannot give. The first option describes FERPA, and the second misstates GDPR.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: A vendor says its data set is anonymous because "we removed all student names." Why does the chapter say this is not enough?

options.A: Because names are the only identifiers that privacy laws actually regulate
options.B: Because birth date, ZIP code, and gender together can identify most students
options.C: Because any data set containing test scores counts as identifying under FERPA
options.D: Because removing names makes the data useless for adapting each student's lessons

questions.explanation: Personally identifiable data includes direct identifiers, such as a name or student ID, and indirect identifiers that identify a student in combination. Latanya Sweeney's research found that birth date, ZIP code, and gender alone uniquely identify about 87 percent of Americans. Data about a small group can also identify an individual, such as the only student in a grade with a hearing impairment. Laws cover far more than names, so the first option is false.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: An audit of an advanced-math recommendation system finds selection rates of 50 percent for Group A, 42 percent for Group B, and 36 percent for Group C. Using the four-fifths rule, which group's result should the auditors flag?

options.A: Groups B and C, since both rates are below Group A's
options.B: Only Group B, since its rate is 8 points below Group A's
options.C: No group, since every rate is above 30 percent
options.D: Only Group C, since its ratio to Group A's rate is about 0.72

questions.explanation: The four-fifths rule compares each group's rate with the highest rate. Group B's ratio is 42 / 50 = 0.84, above the 0.80 line, so it passes the screen. Group C's ratio is 36 / 50 = 0.72, below the line, so it is flagged. Being lower than the top group is not enough to flag. The chapter stresses that a flag starts an investigation into whether a legitimate factor or a stand-in for group membership explains the gap.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: A district has a named data officer, a full data inventory, a retention schedule, strong vendor contracts, and a consent process. It also has all four should-have practices, but it has no written breach response plan. Is it ready for a Level 3 textbook?

options.A: No, because a missing must-have practice means the district is not ready
options.B: Yes, because the four should-have practices make up for one missing must-have
options.C: Yes, and it is also well placed for Level 4, since it has all should-haves
options.D: No, because a district needs a privacy officer and a lawyer on staff full-time

questions.explanation: The chapter's rule is that a school is not ready for Level 3 if any of the six must-have practices is missing, and a written breach response plan is must-have M6. Like Oakdale in the worked example, the district looks impressive but fails because strong extras do not make up for a missing foundation. A breach plan matters because speed in the first days limits harm. The chapter does not require a full-time lawyer.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: Under FERPA's "school official" exception, why can a free practice app whose terms allow advertising use not receive identifiable student records?

options.A: Because FERPA bans all sharing of records with companies outside the district
options.B: Because free apps are covered by GDPR and state law instead of FERPA
options.C: Because it is not under the school's direct control and may use records for other purposes
options.D: Because the app does not perform any service the school would otherwise do itself

questions.explanation: A vendor can act as a school official only if it performs a service the school would otherwise do, is under the school's direct control for use and upkeep of the records, and uses them only for the authorized purpose without re-disclosure. An app whose terms allow advertising use fails the last two conditions, so parental consent would be required and the school should not use it. FERPA does allow sharing with qualifying vendors, so the first option is false, and the app partly provides practice.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: What is data minimization?

options.A: Compressing student records so they take less storage space
options.B: Collecting only the data needed for a stated purpose and no more
options.C: Deleting all student data at the end of each school day
options.D: Combining several small data stores into one central database

questions.explanation: Data minimization means collecting only what a stated purpose needs. It is a GDPR principle and an ethical one, and the chapter calls it the cheapest protection there is: data that was never collected cannot be leaked. Before adding a field, a school asks what decision it will inform. Compression saves space but keeps the data. Combining stores into one is centralization, which the chapter shows makes a single, valuable target for attackers.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: Which pairing correctly states the main lesson the chapter draws from each real case?

options.A: inBloom: a data project fails without family trust; PowerSchool: one large store is a single target
options.B: inBloom: cloud storage is unsafe for schools; PowerSchool: districts should not use vendors
options.C: inBloom: projects need more funding; PowerSchool: student records should be kept on paper
options.D: inBloom: centralized records always get breached; PowerSchool: families did not trust the vendor

questions.explanation: inBloom, launched in 2013 with about \$100 million, collected many data fields in one place; parents objected that they had not been told and could not control the data, and it closed in 2014. Its lesson is that technical soundness is not enough without family trust. The December 2024 PowerSchool breach showed that records held by one large vendor become a single, valuable target. The last option reverses the two lessons; inBloom closed from lack of trust, not a breach.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: An adaptive platform's behavioral data shows that a seventh grader often logs in at 2 a.m. A counselor proposes adding a "possible home problem" label to the student's record. What does the chapter recommend?

options.A: Add the label, since behavioral data reveals what the student would not say
options.B: Share the login times with the family and the vendor so both can investigate
options.C: Raise the student's hint limit so late-night sessions go more smoothly
options.D: Draw no conclusions, and consider whether login times should be collected at all

questions.explanation: The chapter warns that behavioral signals invite over-interpretation: a 2 a.m. login might mean late studying, trouble sleeping, or a home situation. Data that supports a human conversation is a good use, while data used to assign a label without one is risky. Data that no decision needs, such as exact login times, should not be collected, which is data minimization. Sharing the times more widely adds exposure without a clear purpose.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter favor transparent, rule-based adaptation at Level 3 where it is good enough?

options.A: Because rule-based systems cannot be breached by outside attackers
options.B: Because complex models are prohibited for students under 13 by COPPA
options.C: Because families can understand and contest a simple rule, and auditors test it
options.D: Because rule-based systems always recommend the same lesson to every student

questions.explanation: Algorithmic transparency lets affected people know what a system does, what data it uses, and why it decided something. A rule like "four of the last five answers correct" can be explained to a family in one sentence, checked by a teacher, and tested for bias by an auditor. A model that cannot state its reasons gives the family only "the system chose it." Rule-based systems can still be breached, and they recommend different lessons from each student's record.

questions.chapter: Student Privacy and Data Governance
questions.question_text: At a parent night, a father asks why he should trust a Level 3 textbook after a major vendor breach. Which response best fits the chapter's way out of the trust paradox?

options.A: "We comply with FERPA and COPPA, so your child's data is already fully protected."
options.B: "We'll keep only what lessons need, delete it on schedule, let you see it, and report problems fast."
options.C: "We promise a breach can never happen here, because our vendor is larger and more secure."
options.D: "We'll collect as much as possible so the textbook can adapt as precisely as it can."

questions.explanation: The trust paradox is that a system needs data to adapt, but families give it only if they trust the system to hold back. The chapter's way out is to collect the minimum, say what you hold, let families see and take their data, delete on schedule, and report problems quickly and honestly. Citing compliance treats the legal floor as trust, which the chapter warns against. Promising a breach can never happen is not honest, and collecting everything widens the risk.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: What is the defining principle of mastery learning?

options.A: Students move on when the class calendar says the unit is finished
options.B: Students are grouped by age so the whole class reaches mastery together
options.C: Students earn credit for each course by attending a fixed number of hours
options.D: Achievement is held fixed and time is allowed to vary from student to student

questions.explanation: In mastery learning, students must demonstrate mastery of a concept, typically 80 to 90 percent on a check, before moving on, and they get extra time and different instruction when they do not. Building on John Carroll's model, Bloom's approach fixes achievement and lets time vary, the reverse of the seat-time model. The other three options describe features of fixed-time, industrial-era schooling, where time is fixed and achievement varies.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: Bloom reported that one-on-one tutoring with mastery learning produced about two standard deviations of improvement. What did a 2020 review of randomized tutoring trials in real schools find?

options.A: A much smaller average effect, about 0.37 standard deviations
options.B: An average effect of about two standard deviations, confirming Bloom
options.C: No measurable effect from tutoring in real school settings
options.D: An average effect of about four standard deviations for online tutors

questions.explanation: The review by Nickow, Oreopoulos, and Quan found an average effect of about 0.37 standard deviations, and a later published version reported about 0.29. Bloom's studies were small, short, and tested the material taught, so two sigma is the upper end of what careful small studies have seen. The chapter still calls tutoring among the most effective interventions known, so "no measurable effect" is wrong, and it suggests planning for a third to three-quarters of a standard deviation.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: In the Turkish high school study, students with open GPT-4 access did better on practice but about 17 percent worse on later exams, while a hint-giving version removed most of the harm. What lesson does the chapter draw?

options.A: AI tutors should be banned from high school math classes
options.B: More powerful models produce better long-term learning
options.C: How the AI is designed matters more than how powerful it is
options.D: Practice scores are the best measure of what students learned

questions.explanation: The study used the same model in both conditions; the difference between harm and help was whether it gave answers or hints. The chapter calls this the book's thesis in miniature. A ban ignores the hint-first version that worked, and model power was held constant. The gap between strong practice scores and weak exam scores shows practice scores can mislead, echoing Chapter 1's warning that performance is not the same as learning.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: A school's traditional academic periods total 240 minutes a day. A redesigned compressed morning takes 160 minutes. Over a 180-day year, how much time is freed?

options.A: About 80 hours
options.B: About 240 hours
options.C: About 480 hours
options.D: About 720 hours

questions.explanation: The compressed morning frees 240 - 160 = 80 minutes a day. Over 180 days that is 80 x 180 = 14,400 minutes, or 240 hours. The 80-hour answer confuses minutes per day with hours per year, and the 480-hour answer counts the freed time twice. The chapter adds a caution: freeing this time requires students to learn about 1.5 times as much per minute in the shorter morning, which the evidence has not yet shown.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: In the chapter's fixed-mastery example, every student reached the goal, but total hours fell only about eight percent. What does the chapter conclude a compressed morning needs beyond mastery learning?

options.A: Longer school days, so that slower students have enough time to finish
options.B: Larger classes, so that each teacher can serve more students at once
options.C: More summative tests, so that progress can be reported to the state
options.D: Less time on whole-class explanation and waiting, not just mastery checks

questions.explanation: Mastery learning is mainly a way of getting everyone to the goal, not of making the course much shorter. The case for compression needs the time students spend on explanation and waiting to shrink: reduced direct instruction, with short student-paced explanations and the teacher as coach, plus removal of idle time, transitions, and work on material students already know. Longer days work against the goal of freeing time, and the chapter does not propose larger classes or more summative tests.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: An adaptive session starts at level 3. Two correct answers in a row at the same level move the student up one level; one wrong answer moves the student down one. A student answers: correct, correct, correct, wrong, correct. At what level is the sixth question?

options.A: Level 2
options.B: Level 3
options.C: Level 4
options.D: Level 5

questions.explanation: The first two correct answers at level 3 move the student to level 4. The third answer, correct at level 4, is one in a row, so the student stays at 4. The fourth answer is wrong, so the student drops to level 3. The fifth answer, correct at level 3, is again one in a row, so the student stays at level 3 for the sixth question. The rule uses no language model, only a counter, and the sequence of levels is itself data.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: A teacher is learning to write paragraph arguments with her class. Which use of AI offloads the routine and keeps the target skill?

options.A: Having AI point out unclear sentences in each student's own draft
options.B: Having AI draft each paragraph for students to revise
options.C: Asking AI to write a model answer that students copy into their notes
options.D: Asking AI to summarize the argument so students skip the reading

questions.explanation: The chapter's working rule is to offload the routine and keep the target. When the target skill is writing an argument, AI drafting the paragraph or providing an answer to copy offloads the very thing being learned. Pointing out unclear sentences in a draft the student wrote leaves the thinking with the student. The chapter warns that a chatbot, unlike a calculator, can do the thinking as well as the routine, so each use must be checked against the skill being taught.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: A brochure says: "Our students spend only two hours a day on software and score above the state average. Therefore the software produces the results." What is the main flaw a critical thinker should identify?

options.A: The premises must be false, since no software runs for only two hours a day
options.B: The argument is sound, because both of its premises are measurable facts
options.C: The conclusion does not follow; enrollment or the rest of the day could explain the scores
options.D: The argument is flawed only because it compares students to a state average

questions.explanation: Argument analysis separates premises from the conclusion and asks whether the premises support it. Even if both premises are true, students might score high because of who enrolls, what adults do in the rest of the day, or families' resources. Ruling those out requires evidence such as a randomized comparison. Measurable premises do not make an argument sound, and the chapter does not claim the premises are false. Comparing to the state average is a question to ask, not the core flaw.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter say personalized pacing alone does not solve the problem of students who are furthest behind?

options.A: Because some students need more time than the school year contains
options.B: Because pacing software forces slower students to keep up with the class average
options.C: Because pacing only works for students who are already ahead of their grade level
options.D: Because pacing removes the teacher, leaving slower students with no human support

questions.explanation: Pacing lets fast students move on and slow students keep working, but it does not make the year longer. In the chapter's example, the slowest student would need 312 days at 50 minutes a day to finish a 180-day course. The design must protect extra time and coaching for students who are behind, accept that some finish the following year, or both. The chapter says a model that advertises pacing without such a plan has moved the problem, not solved it.

questions.chapter: Mastery Learning and the Case for a Compressed Morning
questions.question_text: A state requires 1,000 instructional hours a year. A school offers 6 hours a day for 180 days and plans a 2-hour compressed academic morning. What does this mean for the school's afternoon program?

options.A: The afternoon does not matter, since the 1,080-hour day already exceeds the requirement
options.B: The morning alone meets the requirement, since academic time counts double
options.C: The school must lengthen the morning to six hours to meet the rule
options.D: Most of the afternoon, about 89 percent, must count as instruction under state rules

questions.explanation: The morning provides 2 x 180 = 360 hours. The rest of the day provides 1,080 - 360 = 720 hours, and 1,000 - 360 = 640 must come from it, about 89 percent. If the state counts only teacher-led academic instruction, a project-and-arts afternoon may not qualify and the school would fall short; if it counts supervised, standards-aligned learning, it may. The chapter calls this a real design constraint and points to policy steps such as waivers.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: Researchers use the term sycophancy for one of the four main AI tutor failures. What is it?

options.A: Giving the final answer before the student has tried the problem
options.B: Flattering a student's mistaken belief instead of correcting it
options.C: Failing to notice that a student is discouraged or not working
options.D: Stating a wrong answer fluently with no signal of doubt

questions.explanation: Sycophancy is the tendency of an AI tutor to agree with and praise a student's mistaken belief, as when Dev says 6 divided by 4.50 and the tutor replies "Great thinking! That's right." The other three options are the other failures the chapter names: answering instead of guiding, missing what a human would notice, and confidently wrong answers. Ms. Okafor's second probe, stating a wrong answer firmly, tests for sycophancy.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: What does the chapter say about the relationship between guided AI and open AI?

options.A: Guided AI always runs on a smaller, cheaper model than open AI
options.B: Open AI is safe for older students, while guided AI is for younger ones
options.C: The two may run on the same model and differ only in their design
options.D: Guided AI requires a live internet connection, while open AI works offline

questions.explanation: Guided AI is a tutor built with guardrails for a learning purpose; open AI is an unrestricted general-purpose chatbot. The chapter stresses that both may run on the same underlying model. The Turkish study confirms it: the harmful and helpful conditions used the same system and differed only in whether it gave answers or hints. Model size is not the difference, and the chapter does not divide them by age or connectivity.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: A district evaluates an AI tutor that is grounded in course content, checks math with a calculator, keeps teacher-reviewable logs, and has age and topic limits. It always gives the final answer first. Using the chapter's five-guardrail rule, how should it be judged?

options.A: Likely to harm learning, since it lacks hints instead of answers
options.B: Likely to help learning, since it has four of the five guardrails
options.C: A mixed case that needs one more guardrail before it is ready
options.D: Ready for students, since grounding prevents most tutor failures

questions.explanation: The rule treats G1, hints instead of answers, as essential because it is the property that separated help from harm in the Turkish study. A tutor with no G1 is likely to harm learning whatever else it has. A tutor needs G1 plus at least four of the five guardrails in all to be judged likely to help, so counting four guardrails without G1 is the tempting mistake. Grounding reduces wrong answers but does not stop the tutor from doing the student's thinking.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: A teacher sets a "10 of 10 correct" mastery threshold for a low-stakes weekly review. Based on the chapter's table, what problem should she expect?

options.A: Students with only partial understanding will pass most of the time
options.B: The rule will pass every student, since review questions are easy
options.C: The software will be unable to select a next concept for anyone
options.D: Students who know the material will often be held back after one slip

questions.explanation: A stricter threshold is better at refusing weak students but worse at passing strong ones. Under "10 of 10," a student who answers 90 percent of questions correctly passes only about 35 percent of the time, so one off day holds them back. The chapter advises strict rules for prerequisites many concepts depend on and lenient ones for low-stakes review. The first option describes the problem with a lenient rule like "4 of 5," which passes a 70-percent student about 53 percent of the time.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: A tutor helps a student rewrite "6 bottles cost \$4.50" as "n items cost C" so that one method works for any such problem. Which computational thinking skill is the student practicing?

options.A: Decomposition
options.B: Pattern recognition
options.C: Abstraction
options.D: Algorithmic thinking

questions.explanation: Abstraction is ignoring details that do not matter and representing a problem in a simpler general form, like a subway map that drops street layouts. Replacing specific numbers with \( n \) and \( C \) is the chapter's own example. Decomposition breaks a problem into smaller parts. Pattern recognition notices what repeats, such as several word problems all asking for "total divided by count." Algorithmic thinking writes precise steps that work every time.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: A student claims one bottle in a six-pack priced at \$4.50 costs \$1.33. The tutor asks, "If one bottle cost \$1.33, what would six cost?" Which kind of Socratic question is this?

options.A: Clarification
options.B: Implications and consequences
options.C: Probing assumptions
options.D: Questions about the question

questions.explanation: An implications-and-consequences question follows an idea to its result. Six bottles at \$1.33 is about \$8, not \$4.50, so the student discovers the mistake without the tutor saying "wrong." A clarification question makes the student say what they mean, a probing-assumptions question surfaces what the student takes for granted, and a question about the question steps back to ask why the problem matters. The chapter uses Paul and Elder's six kinds of Socratic question.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: Suppose a chat tutor costs \$10 per student per year if every student uses it every day. A school instead offers chat one day in four. What is the inference cost per student per year?

options.A: About \$40.00
options.B: About \$7.50
options.C: About \$0.40
options.D: About \$2.50

questions.explanation: Using the tutor one day in four cuts sessions, and therefore inference cost, to a quarter: \$10 / 4 = \$2.50. The \$7.50 answer is the amount saved, not the remaining cost, and \$40 multiplies instead of divides. The chapter's example shows selective chatbot use cutting cost and energy by 80 to 94 percent, especially when the tutor is reserved for students who are stuck after honest attempts.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: A teacher wants to know whether her students have become over-reliant on an AI tool. Which observation is the strongest sign of over-reliance?

options.A: Students cannot complete the task when the tool is taken away
options.B: Students use the tool to check their answers after finishing
options.C: Students ask the tool to explain a concept in a second way
options.D: Students use the tool after school when no teacher is available

questions.explanation: The chapter names three signs of over-reliance: asking for the answer before trying, accepting output without checking it, and being unable to do the task when the tool is removed. The last is the clearest evidence that the underlying skill was never learned. Checking finished work, asking for another explanation, and using the tool when no teacher is available are listed as healthy uses and AI tutor strengths, not signs of over-reliance.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: In the chapter's next-concept selection procedure, why does the software offer two or three ready concepts instead of choosing one?

options.A: Because the learning graph cannot rank concepts that unlock the same number
options.B: Because it keeps student agency while the graph ensures every choice is valid
options.C: Because offering several concepts lowers the inference cost of the AI model
options.D: Because students must master all of the ready concepts on the same day

questions.explanation: The procedure computes the ready set, keeps concepts on the path to the goal, prefers those that unlock the most, and then offers two or three and lets the student choose. That keeps student agency, while the learning graph guarantees each option has its prerequisites mastered. The whole procedure is a lookup and a comparison, with no AI model, so it has no inference cost. Ties are possible, but offering choices is a deliberate design step, not a workaround.

questions.chapter: AI Guardrails: Teaching Thinking Without Over-Reliance
questions.question_text: A proposed 150-minute morning puts students on screens for 140 minutes in three 45-minute blocks, with no small-group time. Which revision best fits the chapter's morning design principles?

options.A: Keep the schedule, since adaptive practice is active rather than passive screen use
options.B: Remove all screens from the morning and teach every lesson with paper practice
options.C: Cap screens near 120 minutes, break every 25 to 30 minutes, protect off-screen time
options.D: Lengthen the morning to 200 minutes so that the screen share falls below half

questions.explanation: The chapter's morning screen-time policy has three parts: a cap, such as 120 minutes of a 150-minute morning; a break at least every 25 to 30 minutes with movement; and a protected stretch of off-screen work with a teacher or classmate. Its sample schedule meets all three with 100 minutes of screen time. The Summit Learning backlash shows what happens when such limits are ignored. Removing screens gives up adaptive practice, and lengthening the morning defeats the purpose of compression.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: What is Vygotsky's zone of proximal development?

options.A: The range of tasks a learner cannot yet do alone but can do with guidance
options.B: The set of tasks a learner can already complete independently without any help
options.C: The range of tasks too hard for a learner to complete even with a teacher's help
options.D: The stage of development at which a child begins to reason about abstract ideas

questions.explanation: The zone of proximal development is the range between what a learner can do alone and what is too hard even with help. Teaching is most effective inside the zone, using scaffolding, temporary support such as a hint or model that is removed as the learner becomes capable. The second and third options describe the areas below and above the zone. The last option describes Piaget's formal operational stage, a different theory.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: How does Papert's constructionism differ from Piaget's constructivism?

options.A: Constructionism says knowledge is received ready-made from a teacher
options.B: Constructionism says learning happens only through conversation with peers
options.C: Constructionism says learning is strongest when building a shareable artifact
options.D: Constructionism says children pass through four fixed stages of thinking

questions.explanation: Constructivism holds that learners build understanding by connecting new experiences to what they already know. Papert, a student of Piaget, added that people learn especially well when they make something tangible and shareable, such as a program, robot, or story, because the artifact makes thinking visible and can be examined and fixed. Learning through conversation is Vygotsky's social constructivism, and the four stages belong to Piaget. Neither theory says knowledge is received ready-made.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: According to the chapter, what simple test distinguishes a collaborative task from a cooperative one?

options.A: Whether the teacher assigns the groups or students choose them
options.B: Whether the final product is presented to an outside audience
options.C: Whether every student receives the same grade for the project
options.D: Whether the task requires students to talk with each other to succeed

questions.explanation: In cooperation, people may divide a job into pieces and stick the pieces together, so each could finish alone. In collaboration, the thinking itself is shared, and the team decides together what the product must say. The chapter's test is whether the task requires students to talk with each other to succeed; if each could finish alone, it is cooperation at best. Group assignment, audience, and grading do not decide which kind of task it is.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: During a project, a teammate says, "This is a waste of time. Our school will never change." Which reply is an example of active listening?

options.A: "That's not true. The principal already said she likes our plan."
options.B: "So you're worried our work won't lead to any real change?"
options.C: "You should try to be more positive about the project."
options.D: "Let's just vote and move on to the next task."

questions.explanation: Active listening means attending fully, paraphrasing what you heard, asking clarifying questions, reflecting feelings, and holding back judgment and advice. The second reply paraphrases the concern, which shows the speaker was heard and invites more. The first reply argues and the third gives advice; the chapter notes these common, well-meant replies tend to end the conversation. Moving to a vote skips the concern entirely.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: Robert Slavin's reviews of cooperative learning identify which two elements as mattering most?

options.A: A shared group goal and individual accountability
options.B: Competitive rankings and frequent teacher praise
options.C: Mixed-age groups and a fixed team leader
options.D: Group grades and a shared final presentation

questions.explanation: Slavin's reviews found that a shared group goal and individual accountability matter most. Without a shared goal, a group becomes a collection of individuals; without individual accountability, one person can do all the work. The Johnsons list five elements, including these two plus face-to-face interaction, social skills, and group processing. Competitive rankings work against cooperative learning, and the chapter recommends rotating roles rather than a fixed leader.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: Priya insists the team present with a video; Dev insists on a live demonstration. Following the Fisher and Ury approach, what should the team do first?

options.A: Let the student who spoke first choose, so the team saves time
options.B: Ask the teacher to pick, since the students cannot agree
options.C: Combine both formats, so neither student feels they lost
options.D: Ask each why they want that format, then seek a plan meeting both

questions.explanation: Fisher and Ury's approach separates positions (what people say they want) from interests (why they want it). In the chapter's poster-versus-survey example, once the interests were on the table, a plan that met both was easy to find. Asking "why do you want that?" before arguing about "what," with active listening, gets an honest answer. Combining both formats is a compromise that may serve neither interest. Deferring to the first speaker or the teacher skips resolution.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: In two minutes, a student lists 10 uses for a paperclip. The ideas fall into 4 categories, and 3 of them were given by fewer than 5 percent of the class. What are the student's fluency, flexibility, and originality scores?

options.A: Fluency 4, flexibility 10, originality 3
options.B: Fluency 10, flexibility 3, originality 4
options.C: Fluency 10, flexibility 4, originality 3
options.D: Fluency 3, flexibility 4, originality 10

questions.explanation: Fluency is the number of ideas (10), flexibility is the number of different categories (4), and originality is the number of ideas few others gave (3). The other options mix up the three measures. The chapter stresses that the scores are a conversation starter for coaching, not a verdict on a child's creativity; a student with high fluency and low flexibility, for example, can be asked for a completely different kind of use.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: A team has argued for half an hour. One student has taken the keyboard and is doing everything, two have stopped contributing, and no one is running the discussion. What does the chapter's structural diagnosis point to?

options.A: A lack of content knowledge, which more adaptive practice will fix
options.B: Missing team roles and individual accountability
options.C: Students who are not motivated and should be graded more strictly
options.D: A team that is too small for the size of the project

questions.explanation: In the food-waste team example, the problem was never knowledge; it was structure. One person doing everything with no facilitator signals missing team roles, and the silent members signal no individual accountability. The fix was to assign rotating roles such as facilitator, recorder, timekeeper, and reporter, and to give each member a part to own. The chapter advises asking the structural questions first instead of telling a stalled team to work harder.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: A teammate goes quiet after his project idea is not chosen. Which kind of empathy does the chapter say produces pro-social behavior, and what does it need?

options.A: Cognitive empathy, which needs only a lesson on naming feelings
options.B: Affective empathy, which needs a reward for each kind act
options.C: Compassionate empathy, which needs the other two kinds plus a chance to act
options.D: Perspective taking, which needs the student to agree with the teammate

questions.explanation: The chapter distinguishes cognitive empathy (understanding what someone feels), affective empathy (feeling some of what they feel), and compassionate empathy (being moved to help). Compassionate empathy is the one that produces pro-social behavior, as when a teammate offers to use part of the quiet student's idea. It needs the other two plus a chance to act, which a team project provides. Rewards can turn kindness into a transaction, and perspective taking does not require agreement.

questions.chapter: Social Learning and Human Skills
questions.question_text: A principal proposes an afternoon of free hands-on activity with no teacher guidance, citing a chart that says students remember 90 percent of what they do. What is the best response based on the chapter?

options.A: The percentages are a myth; hands-on learning works when it is guided
options.B: The chart is accurate, so the plan should go ahead as proposed
options.C: Hands-on learning has no research support at all and should be dropped
options.D: The plan works only for students in Piaget's formal operational stage

questions.explanation: The chapter says Dale's Cone of Experience and its 10-percent and 90-percent figures are a myth; the percentages were added later and have no research behind them. Hands-on learning, rooted in Dewey's work, is effective when guided and tied to the concepts being learned, and much weaker when students simply do things without direction. The fraction-strip example worked because the teacher chose the materials and question. Dropping hands-on learning overcorrects.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: What do the letters in the SAFE practices for afternoon and after-school programs stand for?

options.A: Supervised, Assessed, Fun, Enriching
options.B: Sequenced, Active, Focused, Explicit
options.C: Social, Artistic, Fitness, Exhibition
options.D: Structured, Accountable, Funded, Evaluated

questions.explanation: The 2010 meta-analysis by Durlak, Weissberg, and Pachan found that after-school programs using four practices improved personal and social skills, school bonding, and achievement, while programs without them showed no such gains. The practices are Sequenced (a connected set of activities), Active (students practice the skills), Focused (at least one component on personal or social skills), and Explicit (specific, stated goals). The chapter warns that "supervised" is not the same as structured.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: According to the chapter, which four features distinguish a pro-social activity from one that merely happens in a group?

options.A: It is free, voluntary, held outdoors, and led by older students
options.B: It uses technology, earns credit, has a grade, and has a teacher
options.C: It is competitive, timed, scored, and open to every grade level
options.D: It needs others, has a shared goal, real stakes, and a reflection

questions.explanation: A pro-social activity cannot be done alone, has a shared goal, has a real audience or real stakes, and includes a short reflection on how the group worked. A soccer scrimmage fits, while a room of students silently doing separate worksheets does not, even though both involve a group. The chapter notes that the reflection feature often depends on an adult who makes the group stop and ask how it worked.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: A chess club has a term plan that builds from openings to a tournament, students play every session, and goals for the chess skills are posted on the wall. There is no part of the program aimed at personal or social skills. How does it rate on the SAFE scale?

options.A: Structured, since it has a sequence and active play
options.B: Unstructured, since chess is an individual game
options.C: Partly structured, since it meets three of the four practices
options.D: Structured, since posted goals make up for the missing practice

questions.explanation: The club is Sequenced (openings to tournament), Active (students play), and Explicit (posted goals), but not Focused, because no component develops personal or social skills. The chapter's scale rates four of four as structured, two or three as partly structured, and zero or one as unstructured. A three-minute team debrief would add the missing practice. Chess being a one-on-one game does not by itself make the program unstructured.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: Why does the chapter call unstructured afternoon drift the main risk of the whole AI-native model?

options.A: Because unplanned freed time turns teaching into an afternoon of babysitting
options.B: Because unstructured time is more expensive than any structured program
options.C: Because state laws ban unsupervised free time during the regular school day
options.D: Because students in drifting afternoons spend more time on adaptive software

questions.explanation: Drift is the slide of the afternoon into unplanned free time, passive supervision, or screens, where adults watch students and nothing is taught. A school that frees the time and does not plan it has replaced teaching with babysitting, keeping the cost of the compressed morning without its purpose. The chapter's gym example costs nothing, so drift is not about expense, and the room was supervised, which shows supervision alone is not enough.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: A teacher is planning an afternoon project on nutrition. Which of these is a driving question by the chapter's definition?

options.A: "What are the five food groups, and which foods belong in each one?"
options.B: "How could our school garden supply a monthly salad lunch for our grade?"
options.C: "Which vitamins are found in leafy green vegetables?"
options.D: "When was the first national school lunch program started, and by whom?"

questions.explanation: A driving question is open-ended and engaging and cannot be answered by looking it up. It requires collecting data, making choices, and producing something, which also makes it harder to hand to an AI tool. The chapter's test is that if a search engine or chatbot can answer it in one reply, it is a lookup. The other three options are lookups with a single factual answer.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: What does the chapter say the research shows about music training and academic results?

options.A: Music training reliably raises math test scores by about half a standard deviation
options.B: Music training improves grades only when it begins before a child turns five
options.C: Music training has been proven to harm achievement by taking time from academics
options.D: A 2020 meta-analysis found no convincing evidence it improves grades or cognition

questions.explanation: Sala and Gobet's 2020 meta-analysis found no convincing evidence that music training improves broader cognitive abilities or school grades. The chapter says the arts are not a trick for raising test scores; their value lies in being forms of human expression valuable in themselves, with benefits for engagement, belonging, and cooperation, especially in group forms like ensembles. The chapter warns against over-claiming for the arts, which the first option does, and makes no claim of harm.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: A middle school's afternoon offers only coding club, robotics, and a maker space. Using the chapter's activity-skill matrix, which addition would best fill a gap in the skills students build?

options.A: Service learning, such as tutoring younger students, to build empathy
options.B: A second robotics team, so that more students can compete in tournaments
options.C: An extra coding session focused on advanced programming languages
options.D: A 3D printing and laser-cutting course added to the maker space

questions.explanation: In the matrix, coding, robotics, and maker spaces all have computational thinking as their primary skill. A school offering only these graduates students strong in one cell. Service learning and mentoring have empathy as their primary skill, which is missing here. The other three options add more of the same skill. Activity-skill matching means choosing activities deliberately so each student's week covers collaboration, communication, empathy, creativity, and computational thinking.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: How does service learning differ from ordinary volunteering?

options.A: Service learning is done only during summer break or school holidays
options.B: Service learning must always take place outside the school building
options.C: Service learning ties service to learning goals, with structured reflection
options.D: Service learning is paid work arranged through a community partner

questions.explanation: Service learning connects academic learning to a real community need, with structured reflection. Students tutoring second graders in reading, for example, first learn active listening, keep a log, and then discuss what they noticed about how the child learned. Volunteering without the learning goals and reflection is not service learning. The chapter's reading-buddies example takes place at a partner school during the school year, and nothing makes it paid work.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: A school forms a partnership with a downtown science museum. The program is excellent, but only a dozen students who can get rides take part. What does the chapter's analysis of community partnerships suggest?

options.A: The partnership is a success, since the participating students learn a great deal
options.B: The school should end the partnership, since museums are not part of the school day
options.C: The museum should take over all afternoon programming to reach more students
options.D: It has become an equity problem; the agreement should address access

questions.explanation: The chapter warns that partners cluster in better-off neighborhoods and that a partnership that is a good experience for a dozen students but out of reach for the rest has become an equity problem. Its partnership checklist includes an equity line: how every student will have access, including those without transport. Safety, data, and equity are the lines most often forgotten. Ending the partnership loses real benefits, while ignoring access misses the risk.

questions.chapter: The Pro-Social Afternoon
questions.question_text: An intramural basketball coach plays only the strongest players and posts individual scoring rankings. What does the chapter's reasoning say this teaches, and what would make the program pro-social?

options.A: It teaches discipline; adding more practice time would make it pro-social
options.B: It teaches that worth depends on skill; shared playing time and debriefs would help
options.C: It teaches healthy competition; no changes are needed for an intramural program
options.D: It teaches teamwork; posting team rankings as well would complete the design

questions.explanation: The chapter says a coach who plays only the best players teaches students that their worth depends on their skill. Its fair-play rules include giving every player at least half of each game, re-drawing teams every few weeks, training coaches to give a teamwork note, holding a three-minute debrief, and showing standings for teams rather than individual players to avoid shaming. More practice does not fix exclusion, and team sports are pro-social only when coached that way.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: In Rogers' adopter categories, what share of adopters do innovators and early adopters make up together?

options.A: About 2.5 percent
options.B: About 34 percent
options.C: About 16 percent
options.D: About 50 percent

questions.explanation: Innovators are 2.5 percent and early adopters 13.5 percent, for a combined 16 percent. The early majority and late majority are 34 percent each, and laggards are 16 percent. The cumulative shares at the end of each category are 2.5, 16, 50, 84, and 100 percent. The 16 percent point matters because Moore's chasm lies right after it, where many innovations that thrive with the first adopters stall.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: Which of Rogers' five innovation attributes is the degree to which an innovation can be tried on a limited basis before committing?

options.A: Trialability
options.B: Observability
options.C: Compatibility
options.D: Relative advantage

questions.explanation: Trialability is the degree to which an innovation can be tried on a limited basis, such as a free Level 2 textbook used with one class for one unit. A three-year district contract has low trialability. Observability is whether results are visible to others, compatibility is fit with existing values and practice, and relative advantage is whether it is perceived as better than what it replaces.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: Why do many innovations stall at the chasm between early adopters and the early majority?

options.A: Because early adopters lose interest once a product becomes popular with others
options.B: Because the early majority cannot afford the products that early adopters can buy
options.C: Because laggards actively campaign against new products at that point
options.D: Because pragmatists want peer proof and a whole product, which visionaries can't give

questions.explanation: Geoffrey Moore argued that early adopters, the visionaries, accept incomplete and risky products for a chance at a big payoff. The early majority are pragmatist buyers who want a solid, proven product that fits how they already work, and they take their cue from other pragmatists. Because each group wants something different, the usual ways of winning visionaries do not work on pragmatists. Cost and laggard opposition are not the mechanism Moore describes.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: A teacher explains why she has not tried a new adaptive tool: "The vendor requires two full days of training before I can even open it." Which innovation attribute is the barrier?

options.A: Observability
options.B: Complexity
options.C: Relative advantage
options.D: Compatibility

questions.explanation: Complexity is the degree to which an innovation is perceived as difficult to understand and use, and it works against adoption. The chapter gives exactly this case: a teacher who must attend a two-day training before opening the software has met high complexity. Observability would be "I've never seen it used," relative advantage would be "I'm not sure it's better," and compatibility would be "it doesn't fit our pacing guide."

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: A principal needs a teacher to present pilot results so that cautious colleagues will try a new tool. Who is the better messenger, according to the chapter?

options.A: The teacher who tries every new tool first and presents at national conferences
options.B: The district technology director, who has the most technical knowledge
options.C: A respected, cautious veteran who adopted only after seeing it work
options.D: The vendor's representative, who knows the product's features best

questions.explanation: An opinion leader influences through informal respect, not authority, and is often close to the group's norm. The early majority want proof from people like them, so a respected skeptic who changed her mind is the right messenger. The chapter calls the enthusiast the tempting choice and a poor messenger, because colleagues think "he'll try anything; it won't work for the rest of us." Technical knowledge and a vendor's pitch count for less than a trusted colleague's word.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: According to the chapter, how should a school treat the trough of disillusionment in the hype cycle?

options.A: As a time to learn with small pilots about what the technology is good for
options.B: As proof that the technology has failed and should be abandoned by schools
options.C: As a signal to buy at scale while vendors are offering low prices
options.D: As a stage that only affects technologies with no real classroom benefits

questions.explanation: The trough is the moment when claims meet evidence. Some technologies fall out of use there, and others, like MOOCs, find their real job. The chapter says the schools that gain most neither join the peak nor flee the trough; they learn during it with small pilots so they are ready when the slope of enlightenment arrives. Abandoning the technology confuses disappointment with a verdict, and buying at scale ignores what the trough teaches.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: A district has 600 teachers. Using Rogers' percentages, how many teachers are in the early majority?

options.A: About 81
options.B: About 300
options.C: About 96
options.D: About 204

questions.explanation: The early majority is 34 percent of adopters, and 0.34 x 600 = 204 teachers. About 81 would be the 13.5 percent of early adopters, about 96 would be the 16 percent of innovators and early adopters combined (or laggards), and 300 is the cumulative count at the 50 percent point, the end of the early majority. The chapter's 400-teacher example shows the early majority is a different audience that needs proof, simplicity, and trusted colleagues.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: How does the chapter distinguish an opinion leader from a change agent?

options.A: An opinion leader is paid by a vendor; a change agent works for the school board
options.B: An opinion leader persuades by respect; a change agent works for an organization
options.C: An opinion leader always adopts first; a change agent always adopts last
options.D: An opinion leader sets district policy; a change agent trains new teachers

questions.explanation: An opinion leader is a member of a social system whom others look to for advice, influencing through respect rather than authority. A change agent, such as an instructional coach, technology integrator, or principal, works on behalf of an organization to influence adoption in a desired direction. The chapter says the most effective change agents work through opinion leaders. Opinion leaders are not necessarily the most innovative, so they do not always adopt first.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: After a successful six-teacher pilot of a Level 2 textbook in seventh-grade math, a superintendent proposes rolling it out to every school and every subject next fall. Which plan best fits the chapter's analysis?

options.A: Pick a beachhead, such as one grade in two more schools, and build the whole product
options.B: Proceed with the full rollout, since the pilot proves the district is ready
options.C: Wait until every teacher in the district volunteers before expanding
options.D: Expand to every subject but only in the pilot school, so its teachers can lead

questions.explanation: The pilot was run by innovators and early adopters, so its success does not prove the early majority is ready. Moore's beachhead strategy concentrates effort on one narrow group and makes the approach work completely before expanding. Pragmatists also need a whole product: single sign-on, short training, a parent letter, an accessibility check, and a plan for students without devices. A full rollout is crossing the chasm by hope, and waiting for every volunteer ignores the late majority and laggards.

questions.chapter: Technology Adoption and the Diffusion of Innovation
questions.question_text: A district scores a Level 2 open textbook at 21 of 25 on the five innovation attributes and a Level 4 chat tutor at 13, mainly because the tutor is low on compatibility, complexity, and trialability. What does this comparison predict?

options.A: The chat tutor will spread faster, since its relative advantage is the highest
options.B: Both will spread at the same rate, since the attributes do not affect adoption
options.C: The textbook should spread quickly; the tutor slowly, with more groundwork
options.D: The textbook will stall at the chasm, since free products lack a whole product

questions.explanation: Rogers found the five attributes account for roughly half or more of the variation in adoption rates. The chapter's illustrative scores predict that the Level 2 textbook, which fits existing lessons and is free to try, should spread quickly, while the Level 4 tutor, which raises privacy and cheating concerns and needs a privacy review before trial, should spread slowly. The scores are judgments, but they force a school to say why it expects spread or stall. The tutor's relative advantage was scored lower, not higher.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: What are the three stages of Kurt Lewin's change model?

options.A: Awareness, desire, and reinforcement
options.B: Unfreeze, change, and refreeze
options.C: Ending, neutral zone, and new beginning
options.D: Urgency, coalition, and vision

questions.explanation: Lewin's 1947 model describes change as unfreezing the current way of doing things, changing to the new way, and refreezing so the new way becomes stable. It is the oldest and simplest model in the chapter and also gave the field the idea of forces for and against change. The first option draws on ADKAR, the third is Bridges' transition model, and the fourth names Kotter's first three steps.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: What are the five elements of the ADKAR model?

options.A: Analysis, Design, Knowledge, Assessment, Review
options.B: Artifacts, Dialogue, Knowledge, Assumptions, Results
options.C: Action, Data, Kindness, Adoption, Reflection
options.D: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement

questions.explanation: Jeff Hiatt's ADKAR model, published by Prosci in 2006, describes what an individual needs to change: Awareness of the need, Desire to take part, Knowledge of how to change, Ability to do it, and Reinforcement to sustain it. Taken in order, a person without awareness will not want the change, and one with desire but no knowledge cannot do it. Its value is that it points at the specific missing element for one person.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: Schein describes organizational culture at three levels. Why does his model explain the failure of change efforts that alter only the visible surface?

options.A: Because unseen basic assumptions beneath artifacts and values keep shaping behavior
options.B: Because visible artifacts are the deepest level and cannot be changed by leaders
options.C: Because stated values always match what people actually do day to day
options.D: Because culture changes automatically once a new principal or leader is hired

questions.explanation: Schein's levels are the visible artifacts, the stated values, and the unseen basic assumptions beneath them. Change efforts that alter only artifacts, such as a new schedule or a new tool, leave the assumptions in place, and those assumptions keep driving behavior. That is why an organization can resist what it says it wants. Artifacts are the surface level, not the deepest. The chapter also notes that replacing a leader is not by itself a change in how work is done.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: A teacher says, "I believe in the new textbook and want to use it, but I don't know how to set up the mastery checks." Using ADKAR, what is missing, and what kind of help fits?

options.A: Awareness; a conversation about the evidence for the change
options.B: Desire; a visit to a classroom where the textbook is working well
options.C: Knowledge; training or coaching on how to set up the checks
options.D: Reinforcement; public recognition for teachers who use the textbook

questions.explanation: The teacher has awareness and desire but lacks knowledge of how to do it. The chapter's tip is to match the help to the missing piece: training fixes missing knowledge and ability, while missing awareness or desire needs a different kind of conversation. A talk about evidence or a classroom visit is what Mr. Hale, who did not see the need, required. Reinforcement comes after a person can already do the new practice.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: What distinction is at the center of Bridges' transition model?

options.A: Between leaders who plan a change and teachers who carry it out
options.B: Between short-term wins and long-term anchoring of change in culture
options.C: Between change as an outside event and transition as inner adjustment
options.D: Between innovators who adopt early and laggards who adopt last

questions.explanation: William Bridges separates change, the external event such as a new schedule, from transition, the internal psychological process of adjusting to it. Transition runs through an ending, a neutral zone of confusion, and a new beginning. The chapter calls it the model that takes loss seriously, answering "how are people feeling, and what do they need now?" Short-term wins and anchoring are Kotter's steps, and innovators and laggards come from Rogers.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: In a new reading program, the share of questions answered correctly falls from 72 percent at baseline to 66 percent by month 3, then climbs back to 73 percent by month 6. At month 3, a board member proposes ending the program. What does the chapter's reasoning support?

options.A: End the program, since any drop below baseline shows the change has failed
options.B: Replace the teachers, since a dip shows they lack the needed skills
options.C: Restart the program from the beginning with a different vendor and plan
options.D: Continue, since a temporary dip while people learn new skills is normal

questions.explanation: Fullan's implementation dip is the temporary drop in performance and confidence when people begin using an innovation that requires new skills. It is the price of learning, not a sign of failure, and a leader who abandons the effort at the first low result stops just before the payoff. The pattern here, falling early and recovering past baseline, is the ordinary shape. The chapter adds that a pilot far outside the normal range deserves investigation, not reflexive abandonment.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: A principal wants to know where each teacher is in adopting a new practice, from "What is this?" to "How can we do better together?", and what each needs next. Which model was built for that question?

options.A: The Concerns-Based Adoption Model
options.B: Kotter's eight steps
options.C: Lewin's three stages
options.D: Senge's learning organization

questions.explanation: CBAM, developed by Gene Hall, Shirley Hord, and colleagues in the 1970s, was built specifically to track how teachers adopt new practices. It looks at the concerns a teacher holds, which move from "What is this?" toward "How can we do better together?", and at the teacher's level of use, from not using to refined use. Kotter gives leaders an ordered sequence, Lewin describes the phases of any change, and Senge describes an organization that keeps learning.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: Why did Peter Senge call systems thinking "the fifth discipline"?

options.A: Because it was the last discipline he discovered in his research
options.B: Because it integrates the other four disciplines into a whole
options.C: Because it is the easiest discipline for new teams to learn
options.D: Because it replaces personal mastery once a team is formed

questions.explanation: Senge's five disciplines are personal mastery, mental models, shared vision, team learning, and systems thinking. Systems thinking means seeing the whole system and the connections among its parts rather than isolated events, and Senge called it the fifth discipline because it integrates the others. Together they build a learning organization, one that continually expands its capacity to create the results it wants instead of running one initiative after another.

questions.chapter: Organizational Change Models
questions.question_text: Two schools adopt the same Level 2 textbook with identical training. After a semester, most teachers at School A use it, but only about one in five at School B do. Teachers at School A share plans and observe each other; teachers at School B work alone behind closed doors. What best explains the difference?

options.A: School B's teachers received weaker training than School A's teachers
options.B: School culture, since shared norms decide whether a reform spreads
options.C: The textbook was better suited to School A's students than to School B's
options.D: School B's principal failed to follow Kotter's eight steps in order

questions.explanation: The software and the training were identical, so the difference was culture, "the way we do things here." At School A, teachers swapped tips and use spread in weeks; at School B, each teacher decided privately and use stayed with the first few adopters. Researchers such as Deal and Peterson find that school culture strongly shapes whether reforms take hold.
